residue.text: B9 carries the ordinary ten-bracket mark but contains nine. Correct release requires counting, adding the available spare, recounting and sealing over two inspection minutes. The mark is insufficient evidence of correctness. Its cause is unknown and establishes no additional discrepancy.

Active inspection occupies one of five rack places. A whole transfer load must fit together; blockage occupies both vehicle and transfer clerk. Inspection completion frees space before unloading. Source departure and inspection orders are fixed. Each trolley start consumes one of two allowances regardless of load. Extra capacity, recharge and bypasses are unavailable; batch capacity alone proves no labor advantage.

The three initial rack carriers belong to demand and still require inspection: transfer output is nine source unloads, release output twelve correct completed seals by 13. Transfer labor ranks only complete successes. Later request adaptation is unobserved; no further arrivals occur in this window. Neither empirical comparison nor a global optimality proof is supplied.

summary.text: Model-derived candidate, not an observed run: inspect continuously from 0; trolley B4-B7 during 0-3, trolley B8-B11 during 3-6, then hand carry B12 during 6-7. At 6 only B7 remains before unloading; its completion at 7 permits B12 unloading. Prediction: nine source unloads, twelve correct releases at 13, seven occupied transfer minutes and no waiting. Inspection occupies thirteen minutes.

Closest rival: nine consecutive hand trips from 0, predicted to complete releases at 13 with nine occupied transfer minutes. Replay both schedules in the ledger, checking identities, counts, seals, completion boundaries, occupied intervals, rack occupancy and charge. Opposing hypothesis: whole-load blockage adds mixed-schedule labor or delays release while individual arrivals avoid blockage. Defeat the candidate on blocked unloading, inspection idling, incorrect seal or completion after 13; saved transfer minutes cannot redeem incomplete success. Both predictions remain finite-model calculations.
